text: Fully automated supervisory and dispatch control systems are well suited for adapting the vehicle assignments of varying vehicle sizes and modes (fixed route and on demand) as the demand changes throughout the day. Such changes are much more difficult to achieve with conventional (human-driven) ODT operations, compared to AV fleet operational systems, because of the added flexibility of driverless operation. The importance of IRI to enhance safety and operational efficiency and to improve environmental sustainability and energy conservation was introduced in Phase II research. The concept of IRI to enhance AMD operations was originally proposed in a 2021 technical paper at the SAE Business of Automated Mobility Forum, and subsequently included in an SAE journal publication (Lott, Young, and Zhu 2021). IRI functionality may be integrated into the AV’s automated fleet operational control system as part of the automated fleet operations module that controls vehicle performance, enforces AV safety, and directs fleet operations. This is depicted in Figure 24, which illustrates the conceptual parallel between AV fleet management and communications-based train control. However, as noted above, any IRI failure mode conditions such as a power outage that disable the IRI sensing functions and communications with AV fleet vehicles must not result in a cessation of AV operations. Degradations in fleet vehicle performance levels during these failure mode operations, however, may result. Phase III research built on this conceptual framework, particularly the functions of the ASDC subsystem that monitors and dispatches vehicles as a subsystem under automated fleet operations. Each AV fleet would have its respective ASDC subsystem for vehicle dispatch in response to each traveler’s demand call as well as for managing the fleet in preparation for ridership surge flow response. The ASDC subsystem would also manage station operations, including each fleet vehicle’s station berth (or curb) assignment and coordination. In addition, it would adjust the operating fleet size necessary to meet service levels throughout the day while sending excess vehicles for maintenance, charging, and storage. The ASDC subsystem assigns and dispatches vehicles into service in response to a specific passenger’s “demand-call” ride reservation. This also includes the aspects of “empty vehicle management” whereby vehicles are strategically positioned at stations or offline holding areas in anticipation of high service demand while allowing vehicles to remain dormant during times when demand is low. 43 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications.
